title: 7 Best Product Availability Scrapers for 2026: Tools That Actually Solve Missed Inventory Updates
summary: Compare 7 product availability scrapers including Anakin, Bright Data, and Diffbot. Match the tool to your inventory…
body_markdown:
Your scraper reports full stock. But the vendor's actual inventory hit zero three hours ago. Those missing updates happen because modern vendor websites don't serve inventory data in static HTML anymore. They load stock status asynchronously after the page renders, rotate anti-bot defenses with every request, and restructure their DOM without warning, each failure mode invisible to a simple HTTP client that only reads source code.


A standard product availability scraper fails silently here. A 200 OK response can still deliver a blank JavaScript shell where the "Add to Cart" button should be. If the scraper never executes the JavaScript that hydrates the page, those dynamic stock indicators remain invisible, and your downstream systems keep advertising products that no longer exist. The business cost is measurable. In a DOSS survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers, 62% said they had already switched brands because of a stockout ([Chain Store Age survey](https://chainstoreage.com/survey-out-stocks-often-lead-consumers-switch-brands) ).


Anti-bot infrastructure has evolved to treat repeated programmatic access as a threat. Cloudflare, DataDome, and HUMAN (formerly PerimeterX) fingerprint browsers at the TLS layer, rotate challenge types, and issue IP bans within minutes of detecting non-human traffic patterns. Basic scraping pipelines that lack real browser rendering and residential proxy rotation hit these walls immediately. Protection is uneven, though. In DataDome's scan of more than 16,900 popular sites, 61.2% were fully unprotected against basic bots ([DataDome 2025 Global Bot Security Report](https://datadome.co/threat-research/key-findings-2025-global-bot-security-report/) ). The trouble is the rest. If a vendor you track sits behind one of these systems, a basic pipeline fails on every check.


The short answer: find the failure your monitor hits first, then pick the tool built for it. If nothing in your stack runs the schedule, compare and alert loop at all, start there, because the other fixes only pay off once something is checking. That is the order of this list. It opens with a managed monitor (Anakin), moves to the unblockers that get requests past anti-bot walls (Bright Data, Oxylabs, Decodo), then to extraction and scripted control (Zyte, Apify), and ends with Diffbot for layouts that keep changing.


## Key takeaways


- Accurate inventory alerts, the kind that catch a restock before it's gone, depend on three architectural decisions. Skip any of them and you get stale data.
- JavaScript rendering is non-negotiable. Most vendor sites load stock counts asynchronously. A tool that doesn't execute page JavaScript will return "out of stock" when 47 units just landed, because it never saw the call that fetched them.
- Proxy rotation is what separates a scheduled monitor from a one-shot scraper. Monitoring products handle rotation automatically: fresh IPs, session management, retry logic. Raw scraping tools leave you to build and maintain that layer, which is where most DIY setups break without anyone noticing.
- Structured JSON output removes the maintenance trap. When your parser depends on CSS selectors or XPath, every upstream redesign snaps it. Tools that extract structured data from the page's meaning (headings, regions, table relationships) survive those changes.
- Pick based on your primary failure mode. If anti-bot defenses are killing your requests, prioritize proxy intelligence (Bright Data, Oxylabs). If visual page changes are trashing your parsers, prioritize AI-powered extraction (Diffbot, or an Anakin specific_data monitor if you also need the schedule and alerts). If the orchestration layer is entirely missing (scheduling, state tracking, alert routing), pick a managed monitor (Anakin).


## 1. Anakin Website Monitoring API


Anakin's Website Monitoring API addresses the most common cause of missed stock updates: most scraper setups skip the two layers that produce results, scheduled JavaScript rendering and managed anti-bot bypass. The API polls vendor pages on a configurable interval (minimum 15 minutes) and renders JavaScript-heavy pages in a stealth browser when you set useBrowser. In specific_data mode you describe the fields to track in a JSON Schema, such as an inStock boolean and a price, and every check compares them to the previous result ([see the create-monitor reference](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/monitoring/create-monitor) ). When availability flips from "In Stock" to "Out of Stock," the API fires alerts to any configured webhook or email address (Slack, Discord and Telegram are planned).


You deploy no custom retry logic. No CAPTCHA-solving middleware. No IP-ban recovery code.


Those three elements, the scheduling engine, the browser rendering layer, and the comparison logic, sit inside the API, not in a pile of scripts you maintain. The billing model aligns with high-frequency monitoring rather than penalizing it. Credits deduct only on successful jobs.


Failed requests cost nothing. A specific_data check costs 3 credits (4 with AI change filtering on), so one SKU checked hourly uses about 2,160 credits a month. That fits a few dozen hourly SKUs on Scale ($100/month for 100,000 credits, up to 100 active monitors) and a few hundred on Business ($500/month for 700,000 credits). For catalogs in the thousands, check slow-moving SKUs less often, or point one monitor at a category or search results page instead of one monitor per product.


The real limitation: a monitor runs one URL, one site crawl or one Wire action per check. It doesn't click through a color dropdown and a size selector first, so stock that only appears after those choices needs the scripted browser control covered in the Apify section below. For teams whose primary pain is that nobody is checking availability on a schedule at all, this tool removes the entire self-built monitoring stack.


## 2. Bright Data Web Unlocker


Vendor sites returning 403s, serving CAPTCHAs, or fingerprinting requests at the TLS handshake: that's the failure mode Bright Data's Web Unlocker is built for. It's a proxy-first architecture that lets your requests pass as real user traffic, priced at $1.50 per 1,000 requests on pay-as-you-go and billed only for successful requests (as of October 2026).


*Note: Values are editorial assessments based on available vendor documentation as of October 2026, not independently benchmarked figures.*


Scraping challenge Bright Data Web Unlocker approach Typical self-built alternative


IP-based rate limiting and blocks Rotates requests across a residential network that Bright Data puts at 400M+ IPs Static datacenter proxy pool that gets blacklisted within hours


Browser fingerprinting detection Emulates browser fingerprints (fonts, audio, canvas/WebGL) to mimic real user sessions Manual User-Agent string rotation with no header consistency


CAPTCHA challenges mid-session Solves CAPTCHAs automatically and retries with dynamic IP adjustments Manual CAPTCHA-solving service integration or request scrapping


Session state requirements Bright Data documents session pinning (a session ID that keeps the same IP) for its proxy and SERP products; confirm Web Unlocker support before relying on it for paginated inventory pages Stateless proxy assignment that loses session context between calls


For inventory monitoring, know what this product is not: a change detector or an alerting system. It fetches the page. It doesn't watch it. Bright Data lists batch and scheduled collection, but nothing in Web Unlocker compares this hour's stock value with the last one or routes an alert when it flips. You still build that shell above it: a state store of previous stock values and routing logic for alerts. Bright Data earns its place when you already have the engineering team to construct that layer, and the blocking problem is what's killing the existing stack. If you would rather not run two vendors, Anakin's monitors use the same pipeline as its[URL Scraper](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/url-scraper) (proxies, stealth browser rendering, a proxy country per monitor), with the schedule and the diff built in.


## 3. Oxylabs Web Unblocker


Oxylabs Web Unblocker competes directly with Bright Data in the proxy intelligence category. Oxylabs describes it as a patented, AI-powered proxy solution: it selects and rotates proxies, builds a browser fingerprint (headers, cookies, browser attributes) for each request, and renders JavaScript on its side. That helps on chain retail sites that spread inventory across subdomains with different anti-bot rulesets. For multi-step flows, an X-Oxylabs-Session-Id header keeps the same proxy for up to 10 minutes ([Oxylabs session docs](https://developers.oxylabs.io/products/web-unblocker/making-requests/session) ), long enough to walk paginated inventory pages without the IP changing mid-sequence.


For large-scale inventory tracking, 10,000 or more SKUs across dozens of vendor sites, Oxylabs' pool of 177M+ IPs (its own figure) gives you headroom to sustain high-frequency polling without exhausting available IPs or triggering rate-limiting patterns. One catch: output is raw HTML. Structured parsing is a separate Oxylabs product, so with Web Unblocker alone the selectors are still yours to maintain.


Where Oxylabs lags the turnkey monitoring tools: like Bright Data, it is a data access infrastructure product. You still provide the scheduler, the diff engine, and the alert triggers. It fits when your existing inventory pipeline is well-architected but dying at the anti-bot gate, and you need enterprise-grade proxy management rather than managed monitoring.


## 4. Decodo (formerly Smartproxy) Site Unblocker


If Bright Data and Oxylabs are more unblocker than you need, look at Decodo. Its Site Unblocker, sold under the Smartproxy name before the company rebranded as Decodo, packs rendering, CAPTCHA handling, and proxy rotation into one endpoint with a short setup path. You can get it running across a few hundred product pages without a scraping engineer on the payroll. It suits teams that have moved past manually checking five SKUs and need something that handles the technical busywork of accessing moderately protected vendor sites.


At its price point (from $0.95 per 1,000 requests, as of October 2026), it does what it says: inventory pages come back as full rendered HTML, and Decodo keeps retrying a request until it succeeds. The trade-off is the one every unblocker on this list shares. You get HTML, not stock values. The parser, the scheduler and the alert logic are still yours. For a mid-size operation that needs dependable access without building headless browser orchestration in-house, Decodo Site Unblocker solves the biggest failure mode at a lower entry price per request than Bright Data's pay-as-you-go rate.


## 5. Zyte API (successor to Smart Proxy Manager)


Zyte retired Smart Proxy Manager, the proxy product many Scrapy teams knew as Crawlera, and replaced it with Zyte API ([Zyte's announcement](https://www.zyte.com/blog/retiring-smart-proxy-manager/) ). Zyte API handles bans automatically and picks the leanest proxy and browser setup for each site. Its advantage for inventory monitoring comes from the extraction layer, which understands e-commerce page structures natively.


Zyte's automatic extraction for product pages returns structured inventory data (availability, price, SKU, variants) from complex layouts without manual XPath configuration. That speed pays off when you bring new vendor sites into a monitoring pipeline. Anakin covers the same ground two ways: a specific_data monitor extracts the fields you name in a JSON Schema, and for retailers in the Wire catalog, such as Amazon, Walmart, Target and Best Buy, a[Wire monitor](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/monitoring/wire-monitors) runs a prebuilt action on a schedule and diffs the JSON it returns.


Ban handling happens on Zyte's side. Your spider doesn't have to react to each 403 itself. That helps on sites where a single blocked request triggers escalating countermeasures.


For teams already building on Scrapy, the integration is deep: the scrapy-zyte-api plugin connects Zyte API to an existing spider, and Zyte handles proxy rotation and fingerprint management transparently. If you're not a Scrapy shop, the learning curve is real: the platform's full power assumes familiarity with the framework. The best fit is a team that needs managed ban handling and structured e-commerce extraction in a single platform, and already has the Scrapy expertise to wire up custom parsing logic for vendor-specific edge cases. It reduces the maintenance burden on both the anti-bot and parsing layers simultaneously.


## 6. Apify with Playwright crawlers


Every tool so far assumes the stock status sits at one URL. Apify is for pages where it doesn't, and it puts you in the driver's seat. Instead of wrapping browser automation and parsing inside a managed API, it hands you full programmatic control over a headless Playwright browser running on their infrastructure. You write the navigation logic, the wait conditions, and the extraction selectors. The payoff is a tool that can handle vendor page flows where every template-based scraper falls over.


Take a vendor product page that loads inventory status only after a user selects a color variant from a dropdown, then a size from a second dropdown that appears dynamically, and only then fires an async API call to render the stock indicator. A standard monitoring tool pointed at a single URL and watching for page-level changes never triggers that flow. A Playwright Crawler script clicks those dropdowns in sequence, waits for the network response, and extracts the availability data. It handles interactive state that passive monitoring tools miss.


Apify includes proxy rotation and scheduling, so infrastructure isn't a blank slate. The trade-off: you write and maintain Puppeteer/Playwright scripts instead of configuring a SaaS dashboard. Each new vendor means new code. Every page structure change on a vendor site becomes a code-level fix in your crawler logic.


For a standard vendor product page that just needs proxy rotation, JavaScript rendering, and clean extraction, Apify adds engineering overhead without clear benefit. For the one vendor whose inventory page demands a multi-step interactive flow, and where every off-the-shelf monitoring tool reports a static out-of-stock page, a Playwright Crawler on Apify gets you real inventory data. Teams that want to keep their own Playwright or Puppeteer code without running browsers can also connect it over CDP to Anakin's[Browser API](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/browser-api) , a stealth browser with residential exits in 20+ countries, billed at 1 credit per 2 minutes. Match the tool to the page's interactive complexity.


## 7. Diffbot Automatic Extraction APIs


The last failure on this list is parsing that breaks with every redesign, and Diffbot approaches it from a different angle. It doesn't use CSS selectors or XPath patterns at all, since a single vendor redesign can shatter those. Instead, Diffbot renders the page and analyzes it visually, pulling out stock status, price, and SKU the way your eyes would. That visual model holds up when a site moves its availability badge from the sidebar to below the product image. A CSS-based parser sees a broken rule. Diffbot sees what you see.


For teams monitoring dozens of vendor sites where per-site extraction rule maintenance eats engineering hours, three properties matter:


- **Layout resilience:** Stock status extraction survives most visual redesigns without touching a rule. The AI reads availability indicators through visual and semantic context, not DOM coordinates.
- **New-site onboarding:** You don't write or test selectors for a new vendor. Diffbot's generic product model adjusts to the unfamiliar layout on its own.
- **No manual JavaScript handling:** The extraction API renders pages internally. Dynamic inventory data loaded after page paint gets captured without you orchestrating a headless browser on your side.


The AI extraction layer is a line item on every page: Diffbot's Startup plan is $299/month for 250,000 credits, at one credit per extracted page (as of October 2026). For a single vendor with a stable page structure, the premium rarely justifies itself.


Diffbot fixes one problem: parsing fragility. It isn't built for anti-bot blocking, and nothing in Extract compares stock values between runs or routes an alert. Pick it when parsing rules keep failing across dozens of structurally different vendor pages and the engineering cost of maintaining those rules exceeds the per-request markup. Skip it when you're monitoring one well-structured product page: it's too much tool for that job. Anakin's specific_data monitors take a similar no-selector approach, with AI extraction against your JSON Schema on every check and the diff and alert built in ([monitoring docs](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/monitoring) ).


## Conclusion


The tool that stops your inventory scraper from missing updates depends on which part of your pipeline is failing.


- **No scheduled polling, no diffs, no alert routing at all?** Anakin's Website Monitoring API puts that missing orchestration layer in place.
- **Getting blocked before the page loads?** Bright Data or Oxylabs proxy-first infrastructure handles the anti-bot side.
- **Request goes through fine, but parsing breaks every time a vendor shifts a DOM element?** Diffbot's visual AI extraction removes that maintenance burden.
- **Decodo (formerly Smartproxy)** covers the budget-conscious middle of the anti-bot problem.
- **Zyte and Apify** work for teams that want developer control over parsing logic or interactive page flows; Anakin's Browser API covers the scripted-browser case without running your own browsers.


Diagnose the specific failure first. The tool follows, and so does the end of the three-hour gap between a vendor selling out and your dashboard noticing.

## Frequently asked questions


### Why does a product availability scraper miss inventory updates on vendor websites?


Standard scrapers read static HTML, but modern vendor sites load inventory data through asynchronous JavaScript calls after the page skeleton renders. A 200 OK response may contain a blank shell with no stock status. On top of that, anti-bot systems like Cloudflare and DataDome block non-browser request patterns via IP bans and headless-browser fingerprinting.


### What features should a scraper have to keep product availability data accurate?


Three features are non-negotiable:


- JavaScript rendering to capture dynamically loaded stock data
- Rotating residential proxies to prevent IP bans during frequent polling
- Structured JSON output so stock status arrives as clean data rather than raw HTML requiring fragile regex or CSS selector parsing


### How does Anakin's Website Monitoring API detect changes and send alerts?


The API polls a vendor URL on a configurable schedule (every 15 minutes at the shortest), renders JavaScript in a stealth browser when configured for JavaScript-heavy pages, extracts the fields you define in a JSON Schema, and compares them to the previous result. If any field differs, such as availability flipping from 'In Stock' to 'Out of Stock', it fires an alert to a webhook or email address (Slack is planned).


### Which Anakin tool is best for tracking vendor inventory availability?


The Website Monitoring API is built for recurring checks: it adds the schedule, the diff against the last result and the alert routing on top of the same proxy and stealth-browser pipeline the URL Scraper uses. The URL Scraper fits one-shot extraction, when your own code decides when to fetch. For retailers in the Wire catalog, a Wire monitor returns structured product JSON without any extraction step.


### What limits apply to high-frequency inventory monitoring?


Two practical limits come up. Cost scales with frequency: a specific_data check costs 3 credits, so one SKU checked hourly uses about 2,160 credits a month, which is why large catalogs need the Scale or Business plans or a category-level monitor. And a monitor can't click through variant selectors, so stock that only appears after choosing a size or color needs a scripted browser such as Anakin's Browser API or Apify.


### What is the difference between a one-off scraper and a continuous inventory monitoring tool?


A one-off scraper extracts data from a URL on demand and returns raw results. A continuous monitoring tool adds scheduling, a diff engine to detect when stock status changes, and alert routing to notify systems or humans only on meaningful updates, transforming raw scraping into actionable inventory intelligence.
